title: Hosting options teardown - Lyra Payments discovery
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment
summary: Discovery with Lyra Payments to align on performance and unit-economics for an LLM-powered fraud and customer support assistant. Primary concerns: staying under $0.0008/token for 1k daily concurrent sessions, VPC/KMS requirements for transactions, and proof-of-concept timeline. AE+SE present; next steps include a cost model spreadsheet, security pack, and a technical benchmark run on a small sample workload.
next_steps: Redwood to send tailored cost spreadsheet and queuing model (Maya)
SE to schedule 2-hour benchmark run with Lyra sample prompts (Diego)
Lyra to share representative prompt set and traffic patterns (Sofia)
Schedule follow-up week of 2026-10-19 to review POC results
action_items: Maya Chen: Send draft pricing spreadsheet + hosted vs dedicated delta by 2026-10-08
Diego Alvarez: Prepare benchmark infra and run plan; propose GPU config and batching settings by 2026-10-12
Sofia Gomez: Share 500 sample prompts and latency SLOs by 2026-10-09
Omar El-Amin: Confirm VPC peering requirements and KMS provider by 2026-10-09
transcript:
Meeting Header: 2026-10-05 16:00 UTC | Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Rajesh (CTO - Lyra), Sofia (Head of ML), Omar (DevOps), Hannah (Product)

Summary Auto-generated (may be noisy): Go over hosting paths, cost per token, batching, and security. Customer wants predictable unit econ for fraud scoring and conversational support.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Okay hi everyone thanks for joining, we're Maya and Diego from Redwood. How's everyone's morning — or evening, depending where you are?
[00:14] Rajesh (Lyra CTO): Good, thanks. We're in SF so afternoon here. Appreciate the time.
[00:22] Sofia (Head of ML): Hi all — excited to dig in, we need to understand the real unit costs before we pick a path.
[00:30] Diego (Redwood SE): Great, we'll try to make this pragmatic. Quick agenda: current infra and constraints, traffic shape, target latency and cost, then tradeoffs across hosted/dedicated/private and a suggested POC.
[00:45] Hannah (Product): Sounds good.
[00:50] Rajesh: Quick context — Lyra runs payment routing and fraud detection, and we're adding a small conversational assistant for merchant support and an ML-backed fraud explainability layer. The assistant will call the LLM for short completions, mostly 100-400 tokens per request, and the fraud explainability will use multi-step prompts, maybe 600 tokens sometimes.
[01:12] Sofia: Our priority is predictable unit economics. We have a constraint — budget target is around $0.0006 to $0.0008 per token at scale, and latency under 350ms p50 for the support paths. For fraud scoring we can tolerate higher latency but still need throughput.
[01:35] Diego: Understood. A couple clarifying questions: what's your expected QPS and concurrency? Also do you have an existing VPC/KMS requirement?
[01:44] Omar (DevOps): We typically see bursty traffic: baseline 20 qps, peaks up to 250 qps during timezone batch windows. Concurrency for sessions maybe 1k concurrent short sessions. We use AWS KMS and must maintain keys within our account; SOC2 compliance is required.
[02:05] Maya: Got it — that steers the deployment options. For the budget you're targeting, a mix of caching and continuous batching is going to be necessary. Also dedicated reserved capacity helps lock in unit price.
[02:20] Rajesh: Can you explain how caching helps? We saw references to prefix cache and KV cache in the docs but not sure how that maps to per-token costs.
[02:31] Diego: Sure. So prefix/KV caching avoids recomputing earlier tokens when you have repeated contexts — for chat assistants, if several users share a common system prompt or template, those tokens can be cached and not charged as compute every request. Redwood's runtime also has KV cache that stores transformer key/value states for long-running sessions, which reduces cost for multi-turn. In practice, caching can reduce billed token compute by 20-60% depending on reuse.
[02:58] Sofia: Hmm we have fairly unique sessions per merchant, so reuse might be low for support. Fraud explainability might have more reuse.
[03:08] Diego: Right so for the support flow you lean more on batching and quantization. With batching we can aggregate multiple small requests into GPU work, which reduces per-token GPU cycles. But batching introduces scheduling latency; Redwood's continuous batching tries to keep p50 low while improving unit cost.
[03:28] Rajesh: What sort of latency hit? You said continuous batching keeps p50 low — can you quantify?
[03:35] Diego: In our measurements, with reasonable batching windows (10-30ms) p50 stays almost unchanged and p95 may increase 50-100ms depending on QPS. For your 350ms p50 target that's achievable on hosted with small batching windows.
[03:50] Hannah: How about cost numbers — can you ballpark hosted vs dedicated unit cost at our scale?
[03:56] Maya: We'll send a tailored spreadsheet but rough guidance: hosted API has higher per-token list price but no infra ops — at your QPS and 1k concurrency, hosted maybe around $0.0010-$0.0015/token without aggressive caching/batching. Dedicated reserved capacity can bring that down to $0.0005-$0.0009/token depending on GPU mix, quantization, and commitment. Private (VPC/on-prem) often sits between — if you manage infra it can approach dedicated costs but with extra ops overhead.
[04:24] Rajesh: So to hit our $0.0006-$0.0008 target we likely need dedicated or a heavy batching/caching config on hosted?
[04:32] Diego: Exactly, either dedicated reserved with optimized quantized models or hosted with aggressive batching and KV cache. Also model choice matters — smaller quantized open models can be much cheaper per token, but quality/regression risk must be evaluated.
[04:48] Sofia: About model variants — do you support mixed routing? E.g., call a cheap quantized model for standard replies and fall back to a higher-quality model for ambiguous inputs?
[04:58] Maya: Yes — smart routing is a big Redwood feature. You can define policy rules to route by cost, latency, or confidence signals. That lets you keep most traffic on a cheaper model and only incur higher cost for edge cases.
[05:12] Rajesh: Security check: we must keep PII out of shared logs and maintain audit trails. Do you have options for token redaction and audit logs?
[05:20] Diego: We support redact-at-ingest patterns and token-level retention controls. Also audit logs with S3 export or SIEM integration. For keys, we can support customer-managed KMS in Private or Dedicated via VPC peering. Hosted has BYOK options with a partner flow.
[05:36] Omar: BYOK for hosted is partner flow? That adds complexity — we prefer either Private or dedicated with our KMS in our account.
[05:44] Maya: Totally reasonable. Private will give you most control; Dedicated gives isolation and can integrate with your KMS depending on deployment. We'll document the exact KMS patterns in the security pack.
[05:54] Sofia: Another question — quantization and output quality tradeoffs? We've seen some hallucination increase when aggressively quantizing.
[06:02] Diego: Yes that's a real tradeoff. We recommend running an eval suite against your prompt set — Redwood Optimize can call out quantization profiles that maintain acceptable quality while lowering inference cost. Typical sweet spot is 4-bit quantization for many models, but specifics depend on model architecture and prompt sensitivity.
[06:20] Rajesh: If we do a POC, can Redwood run a benchmark using our prompts to show realistic unit cost numbers?
[06:26] Diego: Yes — we can schedule a benchmark where Lyra supplies sample prompts and traffic shape. We'll run hosted and dedicated configurations and produce per-token cost, latency distribution, and suggested batching/cache settings.
[06:40] Hannah: For procurement, how long to stand up Dedicated? We have time pressure — want pilot in 2–3 weeks if possible.
[06:48] Maya: For a pilot we can often use hosted right away and then spin up a small dedicated pool in 2–3 weeks depending on capacity availability and contract. Private on-prem takes longer.
[06:58] Rajesh: Do you do short-term reserved capacity months-wise? We don't want a long-term commitment for pilot.
[07:05] Maya: Yes we have monthly reserved with the option to convert to annual. For pilots we can do a small monthly reservation or pay-as-you-go dedicated for a short window. We'll include options in the pricing sheet.
[07:16] Sofia: Can you walk through an example calculation? Say 200 qps baseline, average 200 tokens per request, what does per-token look like?
[07:26] Diego: Quick rough calc — 200 qps * 200 tokens = 40k tokens/sec or ~3.5B tokens/day. That scale definitely benefits from dedicated reserved pricing. If you have 30% cache hit and batching reduces GPU cycles by 25%, your effective billed compute could be much lower. We'll model this in the spreadsheet.
[07:46] Rajesh: 3.5B/day seems high for us — I gave a worst-case. But the point is to see the delta.
[07:53] Maya: Right, we'll build a few scenarios (low/mid/high).
[07:58] [08:00] Speaker 2 (maybe automated caption): Uh-huh.
[08:04] Diego: Also note network egress and storage for embeddings can add to cost. If you do reranking or store embeddings, that shows up separately.
[08:15] Hannah: Good to know. We will likely use embeddings for merchant profile matching, so include embedding compute in the model.
[08:22] Sofia: What about fallback strategies if capacity runs out? We can't have support outages during peaks.
[08:28] Diego: Redwood supports smart fallback policies: route to a cheaper model type, fallback to a lower concurrency pool, or degrade gracefully with cached answers. For mission-critical paths you can configure overprovisioned dedicated or reserve burst capacity.
[08:43] Omar: Any SLAs around latency and availability for Dedicated?
[08:48] Maya: Yes we have SLA-backed uptimes and latency targets for Dedicated; we'll include the SLA language in the enterprise packet. Hosted has best-effort but strong SLOs in practice.
[08:59] Rajesh: Let's talk about instrumentation — we need token-level cost visibility and tracing from our app through the model.
[09:06] Diego: Redwood Console exposes per-route token breakdowns, latencies, and traces. We can provide tracing hooks and we also ingest APM traces if you want end-to-end correlation.
[09:16] Sofia: Lovely. That helps our product folks.
[09:20] Maya: Okay, circling back to timeline: we'll send security pack, pricing scenarios, and propose benchmark times. Proposed follow-up week of Oct 19th to review results.
[09:31] Rajesh: Sounds good.
[09:33] Hannah: Quick procurement Q — what's typical invoicing cadence for Dedicated pilots?
[09:38] Maya: Monthly invoicing for pilots; annual for committed contracts. We'll clarify in the sheet.
[09:45] Sofia: Are there any gotchas you typically see in pilots?
[09:48] Diego: Two common ones: traffic pattern mismatch (small pilot doesn't reflect true concurrency) and not providing representative prompts. For reliable cost estimates we need real prompt distributions including longer edge cases.
[10:01] Rajesh: We'll share a mix then. Also want to run a small canary with our internal traffic.
[10:07] Maya: Perfect — that'll validate caching efficacy.
[10:11] [10:15] Diego: I'll propose a benchmark config: one hosted run with batching windows 10/30/50ms, and a dedicated run with quantized model on rtx-like GPUs. We'll export token-level billing and latency percentiles.
[10:28] Omar: For VPC peering, is there any maintenance window you require?
[10:33] Maya: For Private deployments we coordinate maintenance windows; for Dedicated we try to avoid disruptive ops and give notice. We'll add a note about maintenance windows in the packet.
[10:45] Rajesh: Great. If we wanted to minimize cost further long-term, would you recommend fleet pooling across our merchant regions?
[10:53] Diego: Yes cross-region pooling and cold-warm strategies can lower costs but adds complexity. We can outline tradeoffs.
[10:59] Hannah: Ok recapping next steps?
[11:02] Maya: Recap — Redwood sends: 1) tailored pricing spreadsheet with hosted/dedicated/private scenarios, 2) security/compliance packet (SOC2, KMS patterns, audit logs), 3) benchmark plan and proposed times. Lyra to send representative prompt set, traffic shape, and confirm KMS provider. Follow-up week of Oct 19.
[11:20] Rajesh: All good. Thanks everyone.
[11:23] Sofia: Thanks, talk soon.
[11:25] Maya: Thanks all, bye.

End of transcript.

Notes: Transcript includes occasional mislabeling and caption noise. Shared artifacts: https://redwood.example.com/packs/lyra-security (security pack), https://redwood.example.com/pricing/lyra-spreadsheet (pricing workbook), internal benchmark plan (link to be shared after NDA).
